label: Model Riemannian Manifolds
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 55 through 84, builds the three constant-curvature model spaces that anchor the whole book. Euclidean space, the round sphere, and hyperbolic space serve as benchmarks against which curvature, symmetry, and geodesic behaviour are measured throughout the later comparison theorems.

label: Symmetry: Homogeneous and Isotropic
notes: Before naming the models we fix the symmetry vocabulary. A manifold is homogeneous when its isometry group acts transitively on points, and isotropic at a point when isometries fixing that point rotate the tangent space freely. Frame-homogeneity strengthens this to transitivity on orthonormal frames, the property that pins down our three models.

label: Euclidean Space R^n
notes: Euclidean space is the flat model with sectional curvature zero everywhere. Its isometry group is the semidirect product of translations and orthogonal rotations, geodesics are straight lines, and the metric is the familiar dot product written in standard coordinates. It is the curvature-zero reference point for the comparison geometry.

label: The Round Sphere S^n(R)
notes: The round sphere of radius R carries the metric induced from the surrounding Euclidean space and has constant positive curvature one over R squared. Its geodesics are great circles, its isometry group is the orthogonal group, and antipodal points are joined by infinitely many minimizing geodesics, the first sign of conjugate points.

label: Stereographic Coordinates
notes: Stereographic projection sends the sphere minus a pole onto a Euclidean plane, expressing the round metric as a conformal rescaling of the flat metric. This conformal factor recurs for hyperbolic space and shows why angles, but not lengths, are preserved by the projection chart we use repeatedly later.

label: Hyperbolic Space: Four Models
notes: Hyperbolic space has constant negative curvature and appears in four standard guises: the hyperboloid, the Poincare ball, the upper half-space, and the Beltrami-Klein ball. Each model trades clarity of one feature, such as isometries or geodesics, against convenience in another, but all four are mutually isometric realizations.

label: The Hyperboloid Model
notes: The hyperboloid model realizes hyperbolic space as the upper sheet of a two-sheeted hyperboloid in Minkowski space, with the metric induced from the Lorentz form. Its isometry group is the orthochronous Lorentz group, making the analogy with the sphere sitting inside Euclidean space exact and structurally elegant.

label: The Poincare Ball Model
notes: The Poincare ball is the unit ball with a conformally flat metric that blows up near the boundary sphere. Geodesics are diameters and circular arcs meeting the boundary at right angles, angles are measured Euclideanly, and the boundary sits at infinite metric distance from any interior point.

label: Upper Half-Space and Beltrami-Klein
notes: The upper half-space model places hyperbolic geometry on points with positive last coordinate, with geodesics that are vertical lines and semicircles centered on the boundary. The Beltrami-Klein ball instead renders geodesics as straight Euclidean chords, at the cost of distorting angles throughout the picture.

label: Equivalence of the Models
notes: All four hyperbolic models describe the same Riemannian manifold. Central projection from the hyperboloid through the origin lands on the Beltrami-Klein ball, while projection from a lower vertex produces the Poincare ball, and an inversion carries the ball to the upper half-space. The dictionary between them is explicit.

label: Isometry Groups and Frame Homogeneity
notes: Each model space is frame-homogeneous: its isometry group acts transitively on orthonormal frames, so the geometry looks identical from every point in every direction. This maximal symmetry is exactly what forces constant sectional curvature and singles out these three families of model spaces uniquely.

label: Three Geometries Side by Side
notes: Placing the flat plane, the round sphere, and the hyperbolic disk together summarizes the chapter. Their geodesics diverge at zero, converging, and exponential rates respectively, and the sign of curvature governs angle sums of triangles. These three models are the yardsticks for every later comparison result in the book.
